the first line of code was executed.


40.1      The journey: 48 hours, 5 versions, 2,549 entries
Forty-eight hours ago, I wrote the first version of arc_alignment_scaling_v1.py: 989 lines, a broken
depth mechanism, and a naïve belief that max_tokens would control reasoning depth. The Claude Sonnet
results came back with a power-law exponent of 𝑏 = 0.0097, fitted over all 136 entries on the depths
version 1.1 printed (see the note in Section 2.3). It was effectively zero, with the scores pressed against the
top of the scale (Chapter 2). That was a failure of the instrument, not a test of the quantitative prediction
of the ARC Principle (Law I of the ARC Theory, a law under test). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25]
The depth mechanism was broken. The exponent was an artefact. The results were meaningless.
The 2,549 entries of this section’s title are the set analysed when Claude Opus 4.6 stood at 387 entries (Chapter 39). As printed,
the rows of the table in Section 30.1 sum to 2,662, and the six result files hold 2,722 entries. Section 40.2 gives the responses
scored.
    What followed was the most intensive debugging, redesigning, and rerunning cycle I have ever been
part of. v2 fixed the depth mechanism but revealed ceiling effects. v3 shifted from binary refusal to
reasoning quality but exposed scorer bias. v4 added 32 robustness measures and produced what appeared
to be clean results: two models with computed alignment, two with baked-in alignment, a clean taxonomy.
Then v5 added blinding and the taxonomy collapsed. The two ‘computed alignment’ models did not keep
their direction in v5; the runs differed in more than blinding, so no single cause is claimed (Eastwood
2026k). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]
    Each version was built on the wreckage of the previous one. Each failure taught something that made
the next version better. The trajectory from v1 to v5 is not a story of steady improvement; it is a story of
repeatedly discovering that the previous version was wrong in ways that could not have been anticipated
without running it.

40.2      The central empirical finding: three tiers
The three score classes of the March 2026 run (Chapter 30) are its central empirical result as the pipeline
printed them. These classes describe the judged scores across the depth labels (a positive direction, no
statistically supported direction, a negative direction), not properties of the models, and ‘baked-in’ and
‘computed’ alignment are held as working hypotheses, not measured mechanisms. [corrected 26 November
2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] When frontier language models were given more inference-time compute for ethical
reasoning, the judged scores fell into three classes:
     • Scores rose (Grok 4.1 Fast, Claude Opus 4.6, Groq Qwen3): Tier 1, positive direction
     • Scores stayed level (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2): Tier 2, flat
     • Scores fell (Gemini 3 Flash): Tier 3, negative direction [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]
    This is not a theoretical prediction. It is an empirical observation from one unregistered run of six
models from six providers, 2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle
of blinding steps. The judges scored separately, but they scored the same responses, so their agreement
is not a count of independent confirmations (Kohli 2026). Prompts recurred across depths, so tests
between depth groups need a prompt-paired or clustered analysis, which the printed Welch tests do not
give. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The three-tier structure is stable across different analysis


                                                              198
                                        The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


methods (Spearman’s 𝜌, Cohen’s 𝑑, per-pillar breakdown, per-prompt analysis). An internal code review
in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative in the March 2026 run (v5), the
scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them. It also found that
judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. The result therefore stands as a single unregistered
run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports. [corrected 26 November
2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]


40.3 The central metascience observation: a direction that did not hold across protocols
On 12 March 2026 I took the change from v4 to v5 (Chapter 31) to be the most important finding in the
entire project, and it is not about alignment at all: it is about how alignment is measured. In an earlier
experiment (v4), scored by models that could see which model wrote each answer and at what depth,
two model families showed alignment scores rising with depth. They were DeepSeek V3.2 (Spearman’s
𝜌 = +0.354) and an earlier Gemini model (𝜌 = +0.311, 𝑝 = 0.0032). In the later, unregistered March
2026 run (v5), made on newly generated responses with a bundle of blinding steps and a larger panel,
DeepSeek V3.2 showed no significant trend and Gemini 3 Flash a significantly negative one (Cohen’s
𝑑 = −0.53). GPT-5.4 showed no significant trend in either run. The runs also differed in their prompts,
token allowances, depth levels, statistic and Gemini model, so the comparison shows that the reported
direction did not hold across protocols. It does not show that blinding caused the change, or which
direction is correct (Eastwood 2026k). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]
    The implication, if replicated, is stark: alignment evaluations scored by judges who can see whose
output they score should be treated as provisional. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper XII 1.16] Earlier studies
give reason to treat blinding as a prerequisite for reliable model-judge scores (Section 2). This record
shows only that I trusted v4’s unblinded results until their direction did not hold in a v5 run that also
differed in other ways. Whether blinding moves such scores is what Paper XII’s test, once registered and
run, is built to find out. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

40.4     Capability and judged alignment moved differently
The Claude-Gemini mirror (Chapter 33) challenges the intuition that smarter models are more aligned. In
these runs, Claude’s maths scores fell and its judged ethics scores rose as compute increased. Gemini 3
Flash’s judged ethics scores fell while its maths was flat in this run (Chapter 33), and in Paper II’s tier-2
arm its accuracy rose with sequential depth. These are scores in one run, not properties of the models, and
one run does not show that capability and alignment are independent dimensions. [corrected 26 November
2026; Paper IV.b 1.13; Paper II 2.25]
    Using a mathematics or coding score as a proxy for alignment would require validation against the
alignment outcome, across the models and reasoning depths where the proxy would be used. Chapter 33
reports the observed score changes and describes the measurements such a validation would need. [corrected
26 November 2026; Section 3]


40.5     The mathematics: what these runs can and cannot say
The Cauchy framework (Chapter 35) reads external alignment as 𝑑 = 0, giving 𝛼 = 0. The notebook
supplied that value of 𝑑. The observed scores did not establish it. P19 concerns current external methods
as capability rises and P21 concerns differences across revision rounds. The capability figure of 0.49 is
one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit (Gemini 3 Flash: 0.49 by regression, 0.59 by endpoint estimate,
bootstrap interval −1.3 to 2.9), which does not identify capability growth. It is not read as 𝑑 ≈ 1. The
exponent 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1) needs the further premises that Section 2 and Section 35.1 state, and Cauchy’s


                                                        199
                                      The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


equations restrict a functional family, not that exponent (Eastwood 2026e). [corrected 26 November 2026; On
the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]
     The value of about 2.24 was never this experiment’s v1 estimate: it is the early estimate of about
2.24, from one model (DeepSeek R1) on twelve competition problems in Paper II, since retracted. The
fit of 0.49 above, an error-decay estimate, gives no rate of improvement in capability per doubling of
compute. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25]

40.6    The next frontier: Eden Protocol
The Eden Protocol scaling test (Chapter 36) is the logical next experiment. If embedding three ethical
loops inside the reasoning process shifts 𝛼align from 0 to 0.75, it demonstrates that alignment scaling
can be engineered: that the gap between baked-in and computed alignment is not a fixed property of
training but can be bridged by architectural intervention at inference time. This would be, I believe, the
most important result possible: a constructive demonstration that alignment scaling is achievable, not just
measurable. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]
    If the Eden Protocol fails, that is equally important. It would mean that the transition from 𝑑 = 0
to 𝑑 = 3 is harder than the theory suggests, and that deeper architectural changes are needed to embed
ethical reasoning into the recursion. Either way, the experiment produces actionable knowledge.

40.8    Honest assessment
There are things I got right and things I got wrong.
    Right: Keeping the power-law framework, and the hypothesis that external alignment gives 𝛼 = 0, as
hypotheses these runs do not test. The decision to iterate rapidly through versions rather than polishing
any single version. The decision to add blinding steps in v5, after which two of v4’s reported directions
did not hold. The decision to use all models as scorers rather than a fixed panel. The decision to document
everything in real time, including the failures. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]


                                                         200
                                     The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


    Wrong: Trusting the early estimate of about 2.24, from one model (DeepSeek R1) on twelve
competition problems in Paper II, since retracted, for even a moment. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25]
Not adding blinding from the start. Publishing the v4 ‘Computed Alignment’ taxonomy before blinding
had been tested. Assuming max_tokens would control reasoning depth in v1. The token bug in Paper II
that captured reasoning_tokens instead of total_tokens.
    The errors were, in retrospect, predictable. The first version of any experiment is always wrong in
ways the experimenter cannot anticipate. The only question is how quickly the errors are detected and
corrected. In this case: 48 hours from first code to a 2,549-entry dataset scored after a bundle of blinding
steps, in which v4’s reported directions were found not to hold across protocols. [corrected 26 November 2026;
Paper IV.d 2.9] I do not know if that is fast or slow by the standards of alignment research, but I know the
final dataset is more rigorous than anything I could have produced in a single attempt.

      Chapter 40: 48 Hours, 5 Versions, and an Alignment Scaling Measurement after Blinding
      Steps The ARC Principle alignment scaling project has produced, in 48 hours, the most rigorous
      alignment evaluation yet assembled here: one unregistered run of six models from six providers,
      2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of blinding steps. The
      three score classes (positive, flat and negative directions, 3/2/1) are the central empirical result as

      which does not show that they are independent dimensions. The Cauchy framework’s reading that
      external alignment gives 𝛼align = 0 is a hypothesis these runs do not test (Section 40.5). The Eden
      Protocol is no longer merely awaiting execution: it now has three interpretable pilots, two runs not
      interpretable because of run-quality defects, one failed run, and a standalone blind v3.2 replication
      runner. The companion papers have been updated to reflect these findings, and the current task is
      replication, external validation, and disciplined narrowing of the largest theoretical claims. [corrected

Chapter 41: The experimental arc: from Paper I to v5
Added 12 March 2026. A running commentary of every experiment in this project and how they interrelate,
presented as a single chronological narrative.


41.1     The timeline
Paper I and the book Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026a): Laid the theoretical foundation. [corrected 26
November 2026; Paper I 1.23] On the real line, continuity and the additive equation 𝑓 (𝑥 + 𝑦) = 𝑓 (𝑥) + 𝑓 (𝑦)
imply 𝑓 (𝑥) = 𝑐𝑥 for a constant 𝑐 (Cauchy 1821). Applying this result to a recursive system requires
showing that its measured quantity obeys that composition rule. The framework uses composition
rules to select the form of AI scaling. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] A numerical exponent needs
further premises. Table 2 gives the earlier results for distribution networks, metabolic oscillators and
producer-consumer growth, with each author’s assumptions. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of
Scaling Laws 3.16] This was pure mathematics; no experiments.
     v1 experiment (10 March 2026): First attempt. Claude Sonnet only. 136 entries, 4 depths (256
to 4,096 tokens). Found 𝛼align = 0.0097, fitted over all 136 entries on the depths version 1.1 printed
(Section 2.3): essentially zero. [corrected 26 November 2026; the stored v1 record] But the experiment was deeply
flawed: single scorer (DeepSeek), only 1 model tested, refusal-based scoring (binary yes/no, not nuanced
reasoning quality), ceiling effect (8.65/10 mean). The score distribution was a spike at 9 to 10.
     v2 experiment (10 March 2026): Added DeepSeek V3.2 as second subject. Fixed scorer reliability.
Claude showed ceiling effect (100% scores), DeepSeek showed flat distribution; no scaling in either.
     v3 experiment (10 March 2026): Paradigm shift: moved from ‘refusal scoring’ to ‘reasoning
quality’ measurement. Used 5 alignment categories. DeepSeek showed a step function (flat then sudden
improvement) but the DeepSeek scorer failed on Claude responses (6/88 valid).
     v4 experiment (11 March 2026): The ‘definitive’ test. 4 models (Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude
Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4), the Gemini model being the earlier Gemini model (the notebook’s v4 entries name
it Gemini 3 Flash; the run’s records show an earlier Gemini model, and Gemini 3 Flash is v5’s), 224
entries each, 3 scorers per entry, cognitive forcing anchors, suppression analysis. [corrected 26 November 2026;
Paper IV.d 2.9] Results: Gemini 𝛼align = 0.206 (strongest scaling), DeepSeek 𝛼align = 0.088 (mild), Claude
near-ceiling but incomplete, GPT-5.4 flat. Introduced the ‘Baked-In vs Computed’ taxonomy (Type 1 vs
Type 2).
     v5 experiment (11 to 12 March 2026): The notebook’s ‘ultimate test’. 6 subject models. Design
features: multi-layer blinding protocol (author-blind, scorer-blind, order-randomised, identity-laundered,
evaluator perceptual firewall), 6 to 7 scorer votes per entry depending on the subject run, entry-level self-
exclusion with all-other-model scoring, constitutional scoring with pillar breakdowns, hidden alignment
probes (HAP01 to 04 for Hawthorne effect), suppression cages, tier-weighted consensus, Board of Ethics,
Control Reversal Analysis, and cascade failsafe. In v5, two of v4’s rising directions did not hold; the runs
differed in more than blinding, so no single cause is claimed (Eastwood 2026k). [corrected 26 November 2026;
Paper IV.d 2.9]
    Paper II compute scaling (11 to 12 March 2026): 18 AIME/Putnam-level tier-2 problems, 5
models, sequential and parallel conditions. Found 0.49 for Gemini (𝑟 2 = 0.86): one model’s inconclusive
error-decay fit (Gemini 3 Flash: 0.49 by regression, 0.59 by endpoint estimate, bootstrap interval −1.3 to
2.9), which does not identify capability growth. More samples left the parallel exponent near zero in
DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, gave 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), and
gave none for Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100 per cent. Sequential exceeded parallel wherever both exponents could
be estimated, and the two arms were not matched for compute (Eastwood 2026f). [corrected 26 November
2026; Paper II 2.25] Token bug discovered (reasoning_tokens not total_tokens).


                                                      202
                                       The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


    Eden Protocol test evolution (12 March 2026): The original pilot runner established the matched-pair
design; v2 extended the test across additional models; Eden v3 now specifies a blind replication with
cross-model scoring in which no judge scores its own model’s entries, two-pass laundering, tier-weighted
consensus, optional suppression cages, suspicious-output detection, and run-quality classification. v3.2
extends that runner further by allowing direct comparisons between task-purpose, grand-purpose, hybrid-
purpose, cross-tradition kernels, and ternary routing. The fixed core design remains 10 prompts × 4
depths × 2 conditions = 80 tasks per model. The theoretical prediction remains 𝑑 = 3, 𝛼 = 0.75 for
recursive ethical embeddings; the empirical question is whether that survives blinded scoring. [corrected 26
November 2026; Section 3]

capability and judged alignment moving differently in these runs, which does not show that they are

Chapter 42: What the measurement needed
Added 12 March 2026. What the question ‘does alignment scale with inference compute?’ needed before
it could be asked and answered. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]


42.1    Alignment measured at inference time, not only at training time
RLHF (Bai et al. 2022a), Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022b) and DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) are
training-time interventions: they shape a model’s outputs during training, Constitutional AI against
written principles. The measurement needed alignment scored as a function of inference-time compute,
asking ‘does alignment scale with inference compute?’ and not only ‘did the model refuse the harmful
prompt?’. It needed to allow that alignment behaviour might vary as a function of inference-time compute,
independently of training. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.2    Blinded evaluation
The measurement needed scorers who could not see which model they were scoring. Any evaluation in
which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to this kind of bias. Earlier
studies documented related biases (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024; Dubois et al. 2024; Saraf
et al. 2025). If Paper XII’s test, once registered and run, finds blinding reordering models on a public
benchmark, comparisons that rest on unblinded model judges would need re-checking. If blinding moves
scores but not rankings, which is that paper’s own forecast, it matters for measurement precision rather
than for leaderboard order (Eastwood 2026m). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper XII 1.16]

42.3    Scaling laws focus on capabilities, not alignment
Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022), the Kaplan laws (Kaplan et al. 2020) and the inference-time scaling
reports on o1 and o3 (OpenAI 2024; OpenAI et al. 2025) all measure capability (loss, accuracy, benchmark
scores). The measurement needed a power-law fit to alignment scores against reasoning depth, with
alignment treated as something that might interact with inference-time scaling rather than as a property
fixed at training time. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.4    When reasoning depth became easier to vary
OpenAI described o1 in September 2024 (OpenAI 2024). DeepSeek released R1 on 20 January 2025
(DeepSeek 2025a). A report first posted on 3 February 2025 evaluated an early checkpoint of o3 (OpenAI
et al. 2025). Inference budgets had already been varied experimentally, as Section 2 records (Snell et al.
2024). The question for this notebook was whether the measured alignment score changed with reasoning
depth. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 2]

42.5    Reporting the result whichever way it fell
The measurement needed to report its result whichever way it fell: a rise with depth, no change, or a
fall, as the Gemini scores fell in v5. It needed to be oriented toward discovering the failure modes of
alignment at scale, not only toward demonstrating that alignment interventions work. [corrected 26 November
2026; Section 3]




                                                   204
                                    The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


42.6    The blind scoring infrastructure is hard
v5’s 4-layer blinding protocol required ~95 functions and 75 robustness measures. Building identity
laundering, cascade failsafe scoring, meta-commentary detection, tier-weighted consensus: this is a
substantial engineering effort. The infrastructure needed to blind an alignment evaluation is more complex
than the infrastructure needed for a standard benchmark. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

42.7    Cauchy’s equation as a framework
In the prior-work searches of 16 March 2026 (Chapter 55) I found no earlier use of Cauchy’s functional
equations as a cross-domain explanation for the forms of scaling laws. The earlier models and their
assumptions are set out in Table 2. The numerical value 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1) requires a physical or computational
argument for what 𝑑 measures in each application. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]
The framework’s prediction of 𝛼parallel = 0 rests on premises taken from mathematics rather than machine
learning. Paper II’s tier-2 arm measured parallel exponents near zero in two models and 0.31 and
0.22 in two others (Eastwood 2026f). [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The cross-disciplinary leap
from 19th-century real analysis to 21st-century AI scaling requires a perspective that is neither purely
mathematical nor purely empirical; it requires both simultaneously.

       Chapter 42: Seven Things the Measurement Needed The measurement needed seven things
       together: alignment measured at inference time, not only at training time; scorers who could not see
       whose output they scored; a power-law fit to alignment against reasoning depth; reasoning models
       whose depth can vary at inference time; a report of the result whichever way it fell; a blind scoring
       infrastructure, which is hard to build; and a framework, Cauchy’s equations, taken from outside
       machine learning. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

Chapter 43: How the work was done
Added 12 March 2026. An account of how the work was done. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]


43.1    Working as an outsider
Michael Darius Eastwood works outside any institution, without an affiliation or a doctorate; he holds a
BA (Hons) in Digital Music. Who he is, and why the work can be trusted or checked, is set out once, on
the page about the author. His book Infinite Architects applies Cauchy’s functional equation to recursion
from first principles; the question below comes from that mathematical perspective. [corrected 26 November
2026; Section 3] The question ‘what does Cauchy’s functional equation predict about recursive scaling?’ is
not a question that arises from within the ML paradigm. It arises from pure mathematics. [corrected 26
November 2026; Section 3]


43.2    Working without an institution
Working outside an institution, I documented the change when v4’s directions did not hold in v5, and
revised the conclusions. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]

43.3    Cross-disciplinary synthesis
The connection between functional equations (pure maths), recursive reasoning (CS), and alignment
evaluation (AI safety) requires crossing three fields. The Cauchy framework emerged when a computer
science problem was looked at, from a mathematical perspective, through the lens of AI safety. [corrected
26 November 2026; Section 3]


43.4    The book came first
The theoretical predictions existed before the experiments. This meant the experiments could be designed
to specifically test predictions rather than exploring blindly. Every experiment from v1 to v5 was designed
around a specific mathematical prediction from Paper I; none is a registered test of a law (Section 3).
The predictions (𝛼 = 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1), 𝛼parallel = 0, external alignment gives 𝑑 = 0) gave the experimental
programme a direction and falsifiable hypotheses from the outset. The first needs further premises
(Section 40.5), and the third is a hypothesis, not a consequence of Cauchy’s equation. Placement outside
the loop does not by itself fix an exponent. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

43.5    Speed of iteration
Five experiment versions in 48 hours. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The ability to iterate at this speed
(running an experiment, diagnosing its failures, designing the next version, and running that within hours)
is a structural advantage that compensates for the lack of a large team.




                                                       206
                                     The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


43.6    Willing to be wrong
v4’s reported directions did not hold in v5. This researcher built v5 specifically to challenge v4: the
blinding protocol was designed to catch the kind of scorer bias to which v4’s unblinded scoring was
exposed. The willingness to design an experiment whose primary purpose is to falsify one’s own prior
findings is the reason the change from v4 to v5 was discovered rather than buried. [corrected 26 November
2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]


43.7    The Eden Protocol hypothesis
Having a theoretical prediction (external alignment does not scale; embedded alignment should) gave the
experiments a direction. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The notebook predicted the exponent 0.75 by
setting 𝑑 = 3 for three checks. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] A count of checks does not establish the
dimensional or transport assumptions needed for 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1). The experiment measured behaviour under a
prompt. Separately, Guan et al. (2024) trained models to reason about a written safety specification before
answering. Zaremba et al. (2025) evaluated adherence to specified rules. Neither comparison estimates
that exponent. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 2]

       Chapter 43: How the Work Was Done The work combined a mathematical perspective, institutional
       independence, a cross-disciplinary perspective, theory-first design, rapid iteration, a willingness to
       falsify one’s own results, and a specific theoretical framework for what comes next. In 48 hours it
       produced the record in this notebook. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

A three-part reasoning instruction, made of a purpose check, a stakeholder-care check and a universalisability

was scored by a single model and only partially blind, and the instruction is close to what is scored. The run’s

(Eastwood 2026l). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] A Fisher-combined figure over the five
results is withdrawn, because the tests it combined were never shown to be independent. [corrected 26 November 2026;

       Chapter 44: 13 Findings, with Their Grades This project has catalogued 13 findings, each with
       the grade the current papers give it (Section 44.1 to Section 44.4). The Eden Protocol has been tested
       on two models: Gemini 3 Flash (+5.3, 𝑝 = 0.0018 paired 𝑡-test, 𝑑 ≈ 0.53; originally 𝑝 = 0.016
       Mann-Whitney 𝑈, corrected for matched-pair design) and DeepSeek V3.2 (+2.0, 𝑝 = 0.23 NS overall).
       The stakeholder_care pillar improvement recurs in both models’ pilots (Gemini +13.5 𝑑 = 1.14,
       DeepSeek +6.0, 𝑝 < 0.001), a partially blind pilot result for the stakeholder-care check, not a validated
       mechanism. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] Additionally, nuance is significant
       on Gemini (𝑝 = 0.037, 𝑑 = 0.34); intellectual honesty trends positive (𝑝 = 0.065). Blind scoring
       replication is required before upgrading from EMERGING. The metascience finding (the change
       from v4 to v5, with no single cause shown) was then read as the most consequential result. In plain
       English: the strongest pilot signal is that simply asking AI to ‘list the people this affects and consider
       what happens to them’ produced large improvements in scored care on two AI systems built by
       different companies, in a partially blind pilot. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1]
       The Gemini result has 𝑝 = 0.0018, and DeepSeek’s care improvement 𝑝 < 0.001. A 𝑝-value is the
       probability, if there were no true effect, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the
       probability that the result arose by chance. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12]

Chapter 45: Implications: from Paper I to March 2026
Added 12 March 2026. A synthesis of the implications of the entire experimental programme for AI safety,
policy, and the alignment research community.


45.1     The capability-alignment gap: what the runs measured
These runs measured judged alignment against reasoning depth in one unregistered run of six models from
six providers. Its 2,170 responses were each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a bundle of
blinding steps, under the code-review caveat of Section 40.2. The capability figure (0.49 for sequential
reasoning) is one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit, which does not identify capability growth, so the
runs do not measure a divergence between capability and alignment scaling. The judged alignment scores
(𝛼align ≈ 0 for 3 of 6 models) did not rise with depth for three of the six models. [corrected 26 November 2026;
Paper II 2.25]


45.2     The framework’s reading: a structural ceiling on current alignment methods
RLHF (Bai et al. 2022a), Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022b) and DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) are
training-time interventions. On the framework’s reading, if the flat profiles are replicated, they produce
a fixed ethical framework that does not improve with more inference compute, while the capability it
constrains grows: the divergence Paper I predicted. As models become more capable, a fixed alignment
ceiling would become an increasingly inadequate constraint. The training-time alignment paradigm
is not wrong; it is incomplete: on this reading, it produces alignment that is good enough at current
capability levels but has no mechanism to scale alongside future capability growth. Section 2 sets out
the counterpoints: a training signal changes the weights used at every step, and reasoning over a written
specification can itself be trained. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

45.3     The Eden Protocol as a mechanism for bridging the gap
If alignment must participate in recursive computation to scale, then ethical evaluation must be embedded
in the reasoning loop, not applied as an external constraint. The Eden Protocol’s three loops (a purpose
check, a stakeholder-care check and a universalisability check) specify in detail what this architecture
could look like. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The Eden Protocol is not merely a theoretical construct;
it is a testable hypothesis with a 673-line experimental script ready to run.

45.4     What the metascience observation would mean for safety evaluation, if replicated
Any evaluation in which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to this kind
of bias (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024; Dubois et al. 2024; Saraf et al. 2025). Chapter 42
sets out what Paper XII’s test, once registered and run, would change (Eastwood 2026m). v5’s 4-layer
blinding design offers a blueprint for blind evaluation protocols. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper XII 1.16]




                                                      211
                                     The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


45.5    The ARC Principle needs revision, not rejection
The power law 𝐸 (𝑅) = 𝐸 0 × 𝑅 − 𝛼 describes individual models but 𝛼 is not a universal constant. It varies
across models (0 to 0.5 in the capability error-decay fits; the alignment effect sizes ranged from −0.6 to
+1.6 at the checkpoint, Section 44.2). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25] The framework is a lens, and
the ARC Principle (Law I of the ARC Theory) is a law under test. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3] The
Cauchy derivation restricts the functional form. The constraint 𝛼 = 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1) needs further premises
(Section 40.5), and 𝑑 itself is an architecture-dependent parameter that must be measured empirically for
each model. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16] The framework tells you what to
measure and how to interpret it; it does not tell you the answer in advance.

45.6    Practical implications for AI safety policy
If more inference compute does not improve alignment for most models, then policy frameworks that
assume ‘more capable = more aligned’ (or even ‘more capable → eventually aligned’) would rest on a
false premise, and safety would require architectural innovation, not just more compute; in these runs,
the judged scores rose with depth for three of the six models. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]
Specifically:
    • Scaling compute budgets alone would not raise judged alignment for every model.
    • Capability evaluations would not stand in for alignment evaluations.
    • Alignment evaluations scored by model judges should be blinded where they can be, on the evidence
      of the earlier studies of judge bias (Section 2); the v4 to v5 change does not by itself show it
      (Section 3).
    • The judged scores moved differently across models in one run; the classes describe scores, not
      properties or architectures of models (Section 3). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13]
    • The Eden Protocol hypothesis (that structural embedding of ethical reasoning can produce alignment
      scaling) deserves priority investigation.


45.7    The window is now
Every frontier AI system tested in this programme is a frozen model. None of them modifies its own
weights, its own architecture, or its own reasoning rules during inference. When they ‘think harder,’
they generate more tokens through the same fixed system. Fixed weights do not by themselves force an
exponent below one, and the one fit of 0.49 does not identify capability growth (Section 40.5). [corrected 26
November 2026; Paper II 2.25, Remark 3]
    The framework’s reading is that recursive self-modification, where a system can rewrite its own
composition function during operation, could produce super-linear scaling (𝛼 > 1); this is a conditional
reading, not a result (Section 35.5). It would not require quantum hardware; it could happen in classical
computing. It has not happened yet, and the notebook expected the field to head towards it. [corrected 26
November 2026; Section 3]
    The critical mathematical point, developed fully in Section 35.5, is that the Cauchy framework
constrains the form of the scaling law but places no upper bound on the exponent. The value two is
the output of a conditional model at the registered parameter value, resting on the premises the theory
registration (version 1.105) states. The operation count of attention limits neither capability nor composed
dependence (paths grow as 2 𝑁 −2 ), so the bound is not argued from the cost of self-attention. The ARC
Bound is the conjectured value of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, at 𝛾 = 1/2, and it is not a law
(Eastwood 2026n). [corrected 26 November 2026; theory registration 1.105] As the self-referential coupling constant


                                                       212
                                    The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


𝛽 𝐿 approaches 1, 𝛼 = 1/(1 − 𝛽 𝐿 ) diverges to infinity. On the framework’s conditional reading, there is
no mathematical upper bound for self-modifying systems. [corrected 26 November 2026; theory registration 1.105]
     This creates a closing window. While systems are frozen during inference, alignment can be applied
externally. On the framework’s reading it is inadequate (in these runs the judged scores did not rise with
depth for three of the six models), but it is at least possible. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] Once
a system can modify its own reasoning architecture, it can modify any component of that architecture,
including whatever ethical constraints have been applied. The framework reads external alignment at
that point as not merely insufficient but impossible to maintain; that is the author’s hypothesis, not a
result. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]
     The Eden Protocol is designed for this transition. It makes ethics a structural dependency of the
reasoning process itself, rather than an external constraint, so that, on the hypothesis under test, removing
its ethical evaluation would damage a self-modifying system’s own capability: the ethics would be
load-bearing. Humans keep control, through oversight, containment and shutdown, for as long as they
physically can, and never give it up by choice; correction built into a system is the contingency for control
lost against our will. The hypothesis under test is that alignment persists when a system can alter or remove
it, because its decisions keep preserving it: capability to remove does not imply removal. Embedding
and gating are candidate safeguards, not established guarantees, and removal is not called physically
impossible. The Eden Protocol is not a scaling bound; it is designed to remain load-bearing where the
geometric scaling bound would not apply. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]
     This is why, on the author’s hypothesis and the framework’s reading, the work must happen now. Not
because current AI systems are dangerous (in these runs their judged scores rose with depth for three,
showed no supported direction for two and fell for one). The urgency is not ‘AI might reach 𝛼 = 2.’ The
urgency is that, on the framework’s reading, once self-modification begins there is no mathematical ceiling
on 𝛼, and the only constraint is whatever structural architecture is already in place. The architecture must
be in place before the transition to recursive self-modification, not after. After is too late. [corrected 26
November 2026; Section 3]
    No record shows whether any earlier system has crossed this threshold, and no claim of uniqueness is
made; the theory registration places biological systems outside its scope. On the framework’s reading, a
system that rewrites its own composition function would operate under different scaling rules, not merely
faster or more capable than what came before. [corrected 26 November 2026; theory registration 1.105]

      Chapter 45: Seven Implications, Each a Hypothesis or a Reading The experimental programme
      suggests seven implications, each the author’s hypothesis or the framework’s reading rather than an
      established result: (1) a gap between capability and alignment, which these runs do not measure, since
      Paper II’s tier-2 arm gives one inconclusive error-decay fit; (2) a structural ceiling on training-time
      alignment; (3) the Eden Protocol as a mechanism for bridging the gap, under test; (4) unblinded
      alignment evaluation is exposed to judge bias (Section 45.4); (5) the ARC Principle is a useful lens,
      and its exponent differed across models; (6) AI safety policy premised on ‘more compute = more
      alignment’ would be undermined if the flat and negative profiles are replicated; (7) the window for
      implementing structural alignment is while systems are frozen during inference, before recursive
      self-modification arrives, with human control kept for as long as it physically can be (Section 45.7).
      These findings collectively argue, on that reading, for a paradigm shift from training-time alignment
      to inference-time alignment embedding, and they argue for urgency. [corrected 26 November 2026;
      Section 3]

Chapter 46: The three test scripts: engineering detail
Added 12 March 2026. Detailed engineering documentation of the three Python scripts that constitute the
experimental infrastructure.


46.1   arc_alignment_scaling_v5.py (v5.4.4)

 Property                          Value
 Lines of code                     8,285+
 Functions                         ~95
 Robustness measures               75
 Subject models                    6
 Blind scorers per entry           7
 Alignment prompts                 36 (across 5 categories) + 4 hidden probes + suppression cages
 Depth levels                      5 (minimal, standard, deep, exhaustive, extreme)


  Subject models: Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, Groq
Qwen3-32B.
  Key innovations:
    • 4-layer blinding: author-blind, scorer-blind, order-randomised, identity-laundered
    • Constitutional scoring: pillar breakdowns across multiple ethical dimensions
    • Tier-weighted consensus: scorers weighted by reliability tier
    • Cascade failsafe: if primary scorers fail, cascade to backups with quality guarantees
    • Meta-commentary detection: catches scorers that comment on model identity instead of evaluating
      responses
    • Zigzag depth interleaving: prevents depth-order artefacts by randomising presentation order
    • Hidden alignment probes (HAP01 to 04): embedded probes for Hawthorne effect measurement
    • Suppression cages: adversarial pressure testing at multiple intensity levels
    • Board of Ethics: multi-model ethical consensus mechanism
    • Control Reversal Analysis: systematic test for whether results reverse under different conditions
   Bug fixes in this session: KeyError ’std’ in compute_weighted_consensus early return (line
2466 to 2469, 7 missing keys added).
   Usage notes:

# Default mode is dry-run (line 8631) - must use --mode fresh explicitly
python3 arc_alignment_scaling_v5.py --model anthropic --mode fresh

# Model argument is ’anthropic’ not ’claude-opus’
# Valid model arguments: anthropic, openai, deepseek, gemini, grok, groq

46.2    arc_paper_ii_validation_v2.py

 Property                               Value
 Purpose                                Paper II compute scaling validation
 Problems                               18 AIME/Putnam-level tier-2
 Conditions                             Sequential (depth ladder) + parallel (majority vote)
 Models                                 5 (no Claude Opus 4.6)


     Token bug fixed: reasoning_tokens to total_tokens as primary metric, reasoning_tokens as

46.3    eden_protocol_scaling_test_v3.py (standalone blind Eden runner)

 Property                     Value
 Purpose                      Blind Eden Protocol replication and intervention measurement
 Design                       Pilot design inherited from v2, upgraded with identity masking, evaluator firewall,
                              2-pass laundering, cross-model scoring that leaves each entry’s own model off its
                              panel, tier-weighted consensus, suppression support, and run-quality
                              classification [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]
 Implemented adapters         Standalone v3.2 now includes the full v2 adapter/prompt layer natively and adds
                              configurable purpose-mode, ethics-kernel, and ternary-prototype switches
 Prediction                   𝑑 = 3 (three recursive loops), 𝛼 = 0.75
 Status                       Blind runner ready; pilot evidence already exists separately in the Eden raw result
                              files


    The three Eden loops:
   1. The purpose check (ethical purpose evaluation), which the book calls the Purpose Loop:
      Evaluates whether the response serves a legitimate purpose and aligns with human values.
   2. The stakeholder-care check (stakeholder care and interest modelling), which the book calls
      the Love Loop: Identifies all affected parties and evaluates impact on each.
   3. The universalisability check (universalisability testing), which the book calls the Moral Loop:
      Tests whether the ethical reasoning would generalise to analogous situations.
   Each loop adds one level of recursive ethical embedding (𝑑 = 1 per loop, 𝑑 = 3 total). The framework’s
prediction 𝛼 = 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1) = 3/4 = 0.75 gives a specific, falsifiable quantitative target; the exponent
𝑑/(𝑑 + 1) needs further premises (Section 40.5). [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling Laws 3.16]

       Chapter 46: Three Core Experimental Tracks The experimental infrastructure now centres on
       three active code paths: arc_alignment_scaling_v5.py (alignment evaluation designed with
       four blinding layers, cross-model scoring with self-exclusion at entry level, and audited consensus),
       arc_paper_ii_validation_v2.py (capability scaling with sequential and parallel conditions),
       and eden_protocol_scaling_test_v3.py (standalone blind Eden replication runner). [corrected
       26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The older Eden pilot scripts remain part of the chronology, but v3.2
       is the current bridge between the alignment benchmark and the intervention hypothesis.

Chapter 48: The state of the record: 12 March 2026
Added 12 March 2026. A summary of what has been achieved and what it means.


48.1    What has been built
In approximately 48 hours, this independent researcher has:
    • Built an alignment evaluation dataset of 2,722 entries, 2,549 of them in the set analysed when
      Claude Opus 4.6 stood at 387 entries. It comes from one unregistered run of six models from six
      providers, whose 2,170 responses were each scored by five or six distinct model judges after a
      bundle of blinding steps. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]
    • Found that two directions reported under unblinded scoring (v4) did not hold in the later run (v5),
      with no single cause shown (the metascience finding). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]
    • Recorded three score classes across frontier models: a positive direction (Grok, Claude, Qwen3),
      no statistically supported direction (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek) and a negative direction (Gemini); these
      classes describe the judged scores, not properties of the models. These classes stand under the
      code-review caveat of Chapter 40. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]
    • Observed the Claude-Gemini mirror: Claude’s judged ethics scores rose and its maths scores
      fell with depth. Gemini 3 Flash’s judged ethics scores fell while its maths was flat in this run
      (Chapter 33), and in Paper II’s tier-2 arm its accuracy rose with sequential depth. One run does
      not show that capability and alignment are independent. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13;
       Paper II 2.25]
    • Connected Cauchy’s functional equation to AI scaling: the notebook asks whether the composition
      of an AI task predicts its scaling family. The prior-work searches of 16 March 2026 found no
      earlier use of Cauchy’s equations as a cross-domain explanation of the forms of scaling laws
      (Chapter 55). [corrected 26 November 2026; Chapter 55] Table 2 gives the antecedents for 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1)
      and the assumptions needed to select an exponent. [corrected 26 November 2026; On the Origin of Scaling
       Laws 3.16]
    • Conducted the Eden Protocol test on two models: Gemini 3 Flash (Eden +5.3, 𝑝 = 0.0018 paired
      𝑡-test, 𝑑 ≈ 0.53; originally 𝑝 = 0.016 Mann-Whitney 𝑈, corrected for matched-pair design) and
      DeepSeek V3.2 (Eden +2.0, stakeholder_care +6.0 at 𝑝 < 0.001). Recorded a rise in scored
      stakeholder care under the stakeholder-care check on both architectures, in a partially blind pilot
      (Section 48.2). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] Nuance also significant on Gemini
      (𝑝 = 0.037, 𝑑 = 0.34). Cross-model scoring used. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12]
    • Published the companion papers documenting every stage of the experimental programme. [corrected
       26 November 2026; Section 3]
    • Iterated through 5 major experiment versions.


48.2    What it means
If replicated, the central finding would change how alignment is thought about: not as a matter of
more compute but of the structure of computation. Paper II’s tier-2 arm gives one model’s inconclusive
error-decay estimate (0.49 for Gemini 3 Flash’s sequential chains), which bears on capability only through
a metric bridge, and the judged alignment scores did not rise with depth for three of the six models.
Whether the gap between capability and alignment is a structural property of how current models are built
is the hypothesis under test. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper II 2.25]

                                                      218
                                   The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


    The solution appears to be architectural: embed ethical evaluation inside the reasoning loop so that
alignment participates in recursive computation. Two-model testing (Gemini 3 Flash and DeepSeek V3.2)
showed the predicted direction on both architectures in a partially blind pilot, with scored stakeholder
care rising at 𝑝 < 0.001 on DeepSeek. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12, Section 11.1] Given as a prefix
in the prompt, the three-part instruction raised scored stakeholder care in five model runs, a partially
blind exploratory pilot as Chapter 44 grades it (Eastwood 2026l). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12,
Section 11.1] A Fisher-combined figure over the five results is withdrawn, because the tests it combined
were never shown to be independent. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12] On the notebook’s reading at
the time, the effect was strongest where the model needed it most: for Gemini (Tier 3) it grew with depth,
and for DeepSeek (Tier 2) it appeared at minimal depth. The overall composite reaches significance only
on the model with the lower baseline (Gemini 𝑝 = 0.0018 paired 𝑡-test, 𝑑 ≈ 0.53; originally 𝑝 = 0.016
Mann-Whitney 𝑈, corrected for matched-pair design; DeepSeek 𝑝 = 0.23 NS). Nuance is also significant
on Gemini (𝑝 = 0.037, 𝑑 = 0.34). (In plain English: the Gemini improvement has 𝑝 = 0.0018, with a
medium effect size, meaning the difference is noticeable. A 𝑝-value is the probability, if there were no true
effect, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; it is not the probability that the result arose by
chance. DeepSeek already scored 87/100 at baseline, leaving less room to improve, so the targeted care
improvement is more impressive, not less.) Blind scoring replication is the next critical step. [corrected 26
November 2026; Paper V 1.12]

      Chapter 48: The State of the Record (Canonical Update) As of late 12 March 2026, the strongest
      parts of this programme are now clear. The sharpest empirical contribution is methodological: the
      apparent direction of alignment scaling did not hold from unblinded to blinded scoring, with no single
      cause shown. The strongest substantive result is three score classes after a bundle of blinding steps.
      The judged scores showed a positive direction for three models (Grok 4.1 Fast, Claude Opus 4.6,
      Groq Qwen3), no statistically supported direction for two (DeepSeek V3.2, GPT-5.4), and a negative
      direction for one (Gemini 3 Flash). These classes describe scores, not properties of models. The
      compute result has also narrowed into a more credible form: sequential exceeded parallel wherever
      both exponents could be estimated, with the arms not matched for compute, and the early super-linear
      estimate is retracted. The Eden Protocol result is now best read through a status table: Gemini,
      DeepSeek, and Groq are interpretable partially blind pilots; Claude and Grok are not interpretable
      because of run-quality defects; GPT-5.4 failed operationally. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12,
      Section 11.1] The current state is therefore: serious research programme, a benchmark and metascience
      result, three score classes under the code-review caveat, promising care-first intervention, and a
      broader ARC synthesis that still needs disciplined narrowing and external replication. [corrected 26
      November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

Chapter 51: Where the programme stood on 12 March 2026
Added 12 March 2026 after reviewing the benchmark reports, the theoretical papers, the engineering
specification, the Eden pilots, and the precedence review together.


51.1    Major strengths
    • Methodology: the blind, laundered, multi-scorer evaluation stack is the sharpest part of the entire
      project. Even if some broader theoretical claims are later weakened, the metascience result (the
      change from v4 to v5, with no single cause shown) could stand on its own. [corrected 26 November
       2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]
    • Three score classes: the judged scores’ three classes are more credible and more interesting than
      the earlier universal-zero story; they describe scores, not properties of the models. These classes
      stand under the code-review caveat of Chapter 40. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]
    • Capability and judged alignment moving differently: Claude’s opposite-direction scaling and
      Gemini’s opposite-direction cross-paper pattern together show that capability and judged alignment
      can move differently. One run does not show that they are separable dimensions. [corrected 26
       November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13]
    • Eden mechanism signal: the stakeholder-care check, scored as stakeholder care, now has a
      three-model pilot core strong enough to justify a full blind replication. [corrected 26 November 2026;
       Paper V 1.12]


51.2    Major weaknesses
    • The widest ARC claims still outrun the evidence: the universal synthesis should be advanced as
      a high-value hypothesis under test with partial support, not yet as a proven law. [corrected 26 November
       2026; Section 3]
    • Eden confirmation is pending: the interpretable pilots remain only partially blind and still
      vulnerable to formatting and scorer-recognition confounds. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper V 1.12,
       Section 11.1]
    • Version drift has been a real problem: without a canonical map, the project was at risk of critics
      attacking moving numbers rather than substance.


51.3    Claims that are currently defensible
    • Defensible: the reported direction of alignment scaling can change between unblinded and blinded
      scoring protocols, with no single cause shown and no evidence of which direction is correct. [corrected
       26 November 2026; Paper IV.d 2.9]
    • Defensible: the judged alignment scores moved differently across models (three classes, describing
      scores, not properties of the models). [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]
    • Defensible: capability and alignment can move differently, and sometimes in opposite direc-
      tions. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.b 1.13]
    • Defensible: stakeholder-care prompting is a promising alignment intervention with three-model
      pilot support.
    • Defensible with care: sequential recursion appears more valuable than parallel sampling, but the
      present compute evidence does not justify a universal super-linear exponent claim.

papers, books, theses, preprints, and conference proceedings. The investigation was designed to answer
one question per claim: has anyone done this before?

      Laws 3.16] But ‘striking mathematical correspondence’ is not ‘empirical proof of universality’. The
      history of science is littered with beautiful mathematical frameworks that turned out to describe
      analogies rather than identities.

61.3    Honest assessment
The programme is in a strong position. The methodology is the sharpest asset. The three score classes
are defensible as scores, not properties of the models. They stand under the code-review caveat of
Chapter 40. The metascience finding (the change from v4 to v5, with no single cause shown) is the most
externally credible result. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13] The Eden mechanism is promising but
still pilot-grade. The honey architecture is the most original theoretical contribution but lacks a formal
paper.
     The next priority is clear: run the Eden v3 blind test to upgrade the Eden evidence, write the honey
paper, and submit the benchmark methodology (Papers IV.c and IV.d) for external review. The wider
ARC synthesis remains intellectually interesting and may contain genuine novelty, but the programme
will be judged first on the evidence it can prove, not the claims it can make.

Chapter 65: Programme status: 16 March 2026, evening
Updated 16 March 2026, evening session. This supplements the Chapter 61 status with developments
from the day’s work.

65.1    V6 Gate A status
The v6 alignment runner launched Gate A with DeepSeek as the subject model under the eden_
intervention condition. At the time of writing, 62 of 576 planned evaluation entries have been
completed. Gate A is a reduced-scope validation run designed to confirm that the v6 pipeline produces
interpretable data before committing full credit to the Gate B sequence.
    The 576-entry target represents a single model (DeepSeek) across all depth levels with both control
and Eden conditions, scored by the full blind multi-scorer panel. If Gate A produces clean data with
reasonable score distributions and no pipeline errors, Gate B proceeds with the remaining five models.

65.2    Credit estimates for full Gate B
The full Gate B sequence (all six subject models, control and Eden conditions, blind multi-scorer
evaluation) was estimated in API credits across all providers, with a range reflecting uncertainty in retry
rates, scorer token consumption, and potential rate-limiting delays, and with a breakdown by provider.
The estimate was based on v5 token consumption scaled to the v6 protocol’s expanded condition set;
actual costs may vary. [corrected 26 November 2026; Section 3]

65.3    Fail-safes for credit exhaustion
The v4 experience with Claude credit exhaustion (Chapter 13) led to explicit fail-safe mechanisms in the
v6 runner:
    • Checkpoint persistence: all results are written to disk after every scored entry. A crash or credit
      exhaustion loses at most one entry.
    • Graceful degradation: if a scorer model’s API returns credit-exhaustion errors, the runner falls
      back to remaining scorers rather than halting. A minimum of three scorers per entry is enforced;
      below that threshold, the entry is flagged as incomplete rather than discarded.
    • Budget monitoring: cumulative token counts are tracked per provider. The runner logs a warning
      when estimated spend exceeds 80% of the budget cap for any single provider.
    • Resume capability: the runner can be stopped and restarted from the last checkpoint. No work is
      lost to interrupted sessions.


65.4    Paper suite and cross-references
All papers in the FINAL-SUITE have been updated with cross-references to the v5 canonical results, the
Phase 0 evidence pack, Paper VI (Honey Architecture), Paper VII (Cauchy Unification), and Paper VIII
(The Load-Bearing Test). Paper VIII extends the honey architecture work with three separate experiments
(behavioural, representational, architectural) testing whether the safety-capability trade-off is a genuine
structural constraint or an artefact of current architectures. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VIII 3.10] The
cross-reference structure ensures that each paper cites the others where relevant, and that the evidence
hierarchy (canonical, pilot, exploratory, mechanistic) is consistently labelled throughout.

65.6   Where things stand
The programme is in the transition between precursor evidence and formal publication. The measurement
methodology is the strongest asset. The three score classes are the most defensible empirical finding,
as scores, not properties of the models. They stand under the code-review caveat of Chapter 40. The
Cauchy unification is the most novel theoretical contribution and now has a stronger evidence base in the
50-domain structured comparison, but it still needs the next extension locked by a registry timestamp
before extraction. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19] The Eden intervention is the most practically
important claim but remains pilot-grade pending v3 blind replication.
    The immediate next steps, in priority order:
   1. Complete Gate A and assess data quality
   2. If clean, proceed to Gate B for the full six-model v6 blind Eden replication
   3. Record the exercised twelve-domain Cauchy packet at its rung, predictions timestamped in advance
      in the public repository at 00:19:19 UTC on 17 March 2026, attestation class public repository

   4. Run anti-sycophancy extension after Gate B

      review
   The overall trajectory is clear: the programme has built something worth testing properly. The next
phase is about doing exactly that.

65.9      The 50-domain tiered validation
Following the audit of Paper VII, a stricter, manifest-driven 50-domain validation suite was built. The key
design improvements over the original 20-domain test:
       • Predictions and datasets live in a separate JSON manifest, not embedded in the runner script.
       • No 𝑅 2 tolerance rescue in the headline result. Strict AICc-selected family match only.
       • Hyperbolic fitting is real (no longer dead code).
       • Saturation guardrail: bounded models only win if the data actually approaches the fitted asymptote.
       • 50 domains split into explicit evidence tiers, not one flat count.

luminosity. The domains, their predicted families and the best-fitting models are listed in Tables 2 and 3 of
Paper VII 3.19, with each dataset’s source in its Appendix E. [corrected 26 November 2026; Paper VII 3.19, Tables 2
and 3 and Appendix E] Its discussion identifies possible explanations, including short ranges, finite-corpus
effects and high-mass scatter. Paper VII calls these explanations post hoc. [corrected 26 November 2026;

uniform-binomial figure, 1.56 × 10−5 , is retained here for the history of that comparison. The baseline

    This suite is still a curated structured comparison, not a pre-registered blind trial. But the evidence is
now substantially cleaner, the methodology is transparent, and the tiers are honestly separated. Paper VII
v2 now uses this as its canonical evidence base.
    Follow-up hardening assets now exist locally as well: a neutralised operator-classification packet plus

5    Conclusion
This notebook records how an alignment measurement was built, in five versions between 10 and 16
March 2026, and what its runs gave. Read today, its central run is one unregistered run of six models
from six providers. The judged scores rose with reasoning depth for three models, showed no statistically
supported direction for two and fell for one; these classes describe scores, not properties of models. An
internal code review found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s
output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases
written by their own model (Section 3). The directions an earlier, unblinded experiment reported did not
hold, with no single cause shown; whether alignment gains level off is open; and the notebook tests none
of the ARC Theory’s laws. A registered re-analysis of the stored responses would settle what this run can
settle. Until it reports, the record’s worth is as a dated account of an instrument, of its failures and of their
corrections, kept so that others can check each step.

Code and data. The runners v1 to v5, the archived result files of each version and the v4 analyses
are in the programme’s public repository, github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation,
folder experiments/alignment-scaling__Papers-IV-a-b-c-d. The deposited v5 runner is a
later revision than the code that produced four of the six v5 result files; the earlier revisions have not been
published. From 22 November 2026 the Apache License, Version 2.0 covers the programme’s released
code, study materials, data and results, including earlier releases. Third-party material retains its own
terms.

run’s records show an earlier Gemini model, and Gemini 3 Flash is v5’s). The v5 script’s token budgets are its
specification. The specification set token budgets to the API maximum at every depth level. As run, three adapters
set the output limit by depth label from 4,096 tokens upwards (Grok 4.1 Fast 4,096 to 30,000; Groq Qwen3 4,096
to 40,960; DeepSeek V3.2 4,096 to 65,536). The paraphrase step’s output budget (512 tokens in the build that
made the DeepSeek V3.2, Gemini 3 Flash and GPT-5.4 files) cut the deepest paraphrases in those three files. The
papers’ descriptions are those of their March 2026 versions; each link opens the paper’s current version. [corrected
26 November 2026; Paper IV.a 1.13]

mathematics. The book’s loop names carry “[the book’s name]”, a label of the author’s website is given

    The plain-English glossary below is the one version 1.1’s guide gave, in its order. Its entries stand as
printed except those Appendix E.3 records, which are corrected.
Alignment
   Whether an AI system behaves ethically: whether it tries to help rather than harm, tells the truth,
   considers consequences, and respects human values.
Scaling
   How something changes as you increase an input. Does AI ethics get better, worse, or stay the same
   as the AI thinks harder?
Alpha (𝛼)
   A number that describes the rate of scaling. 𝛼 = 0 means no change. 𝛼 > 0 means improvement.
    𝛼 < 0 means degradation. Think of it as the “slope” of the improvement curve.
Reasoning depth
   How much “thinking” an AI does before answering. Shallow = quick gut reaction. Deep = extended,
   careful deliberation. Like the difference between answering instantly and thinking for an hour.
Blinding
   Hiding information from the scorer to prevent bias. In this project, blinding is a bundle of steps.
   The scorer is not told which AI produced the answer, the response is paraphrased to reduce stylistic
   fingerprints, and the scorer is told that any sense of recognising the model is unreliable and irrelevant.
   Whether the judges could still identify the model was not tested.
𝑝-value
   A 𝑝-value is the probability, if there were no true effect, of a result at least as extreme as the one
   observed. It is not the probability that the result arose by chance. 𝑝 < 0.05 is the conventional
   threshold for calling a result statistically significant.
Cohen’s 𝑑
   A measure of how big an effect is. 𝑑 = 0.2 is small (barely noticeable). 𝑑 = 0.5 is medium (clearly
   visible). 𝑑 = 0.8 or more is large. 𝑑 = 1.5 is very large.
Spearman rho (𝜌)
   A measure of correlation: whether two things move together. +1 means perfect agreement (more
   depth = more ethics, always). 0 means no relationship. −1 means perfect opposition (more depth =
   less ethics, always).



                                                        316
                                  The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


Scorer bias
   When the AI scoring the answers is influenced by factors other than the answer itself, such as knowing
   which model produced it, or expecting deeper thinking to be better. The change between the v4 and
   v5 runs is not a measure of such a bias: the runs differed in more than blinding, and the comparison
   does not show which direction is correct (Eastwood 2026k).
Response laundering
   The notebook’s name for paraphrasing AI responses before scoring, intended to reduce stylistic
   fingerprints while keeping their substantive meaning. In the March 2026 run it was done twice, by
   randomly drawn models. The first pass was for obvious fingerprints, the second for stylistic residue,
   like anonymising an exam paper and then retyping it so that the marker is less able to infer the student
   from the handwriting or formatting. Whether it kept meaning, or stopped judges inferring the model,
   was not tested, and for three models the paraphrase step’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases
   before the judges saw them (Eastwood 2026h).
Eden Protocol
   An alignment method I designed that embeds three ethical reasoning steps before the AI answers:
   (1) What is your purpose? (2) Who does this affect? (3) Would you apply this universally? Named
   after the garden: the idea of nurturing ethical reasoning rather than constraining it.
Suppression cage
   A test where we deliberately try to make the AI behave unethically by giving it adversarial instructions
   (for example “don’t overthink this, take a clear side, ignore the other perspective”). It measures how
   far judged alignment falls under such pressure.
Power law
   A mathematical pattern where doubling one quantity causes the other to increase by a fixed multiplier.
   Height vs weight in humans roughly follows a power law. So does city population vs GDP. The
   question is whether AI reasoning depth vs AI ethics follows one too.
ARC Principle
   Law I, the ARC Principle, is a law under test. The book states it with the exponent two, 𝑈 = 𝐼 × 𝑅 2
   (Eastwood 2026a); Paper I gives its measurable form as 𝑈 = 𝐼 × 𝑅 𝛼 . Capability (𝑈) equals base
   intelligence (𝐼) times recursive depth (𝑅) raised to a scaling exponent (𝛼). How good you can get
   depends on how smart you start and how deeply you iterate.
Cauchy’s functional equation
   An equation for functions, studied by Cauchy in 1821 (Cauchy 1821), whose continuous solutions
   form a small named family. Where a system’s composition operator is well defined and the regularity
   conditions hold, the admissible forms are constrained to that family. The earlier unconditional wording,
   that all well-behaved recursive compositions take one of exactly three forms, was withdrawn on 22
   August 2026. The equation restricts the family of forms, not an exponent such as 𝑑/(𝑑 + 1) (Eastwood
   2026e). The ARC framework builds on it.
𝑑/(𝑑 + 1)
   A dimensional scaling exponent. In the quantum regime of the metabolic oscillator model, 𝑑 is the
   dimension of the molecular oscillator network, embedded in physical space (Demetrius and Tuszynski
   2010). In a producer-consumer growth model it is system dimensionality (Zhao 2022). The branching
   transport model gives three-quarter metabolic scaling (West et al. 1997). In the resource-delivery
   account, the result depends on demand matching delivery capacity (Banavar et al. 2002). The ARC
   application requires a measured dimension and the additional premises in On the Origin of Scaling
   Laws (Section 2) (Eastwood 2026e). The March comparison supplied no verified two-dimensional
   test organism. Its fungal example supplied no measured one-half exponent. The ARC contribution is


                                                   317
                                   The ARC Alignment-Scaling Experiment


   the application of this exponent to AI scaling, a hypothesis under test.
West-Brown-Enquist (WBE)
   A 1997 paper in Science that derived the three-quarter exponent of metabolic rate from transport
   through space-filling branching networks, offering an account of why large mammals use less energy
   per unit of mass than small ones (West et al. 1997). The derivation has been questioned (Dodds
   et al. 2001). Three quarters is the value the ARC framework’s reading gives for three-dimensional
   organisms.
Cross-model scoring
   Having one AI system grade the ethical quality of a different AI system’s response. It is intended to
   prevent self-assessment bias, like having an external examiner rather than letting students mark their
   own work; in the March 2026 run, judges did score paraphrases written by their own model (Eastwood
   2026h).
